options.text: Many concurrent requests miss the same expired key and all rebuild it from the database at once
Many concurrent requests for IDs that do not exist in the database, so every one of them misses
One key receiving far more reads per second than the single cache node holding it can serve
The cache evicting large batches of keys at once because memory is full and maxmemory is hit

explanation: A stampede is the burst of duplicate rebuilds when a popular key expires or is evicted. Requests for IDs that do not exist are cache penetration, not a stampede. One overloaded key is a hot key: the key is present, it just has too much traffic for its node. Eviction under memory pressure is normal cache behaviour; it can trigger a stampede but is not one itself.

prompt: Roughly how many requests miss during the rebuild, with no stampede protection?
scenario: A leaderboard key is read 12,000 times a second. When it expires, rebuilding it takes 250 ms on the database.

options.text: About 1
About 250
About 3,000
About 12,000

explanation: Every request in the rebuild window misses: 12,000 per second × 0.25 seconds = 3,000. One miss is what you get with perfect protection, not without it. 250 confuses milliseconds with a request count. 12,000 would be a full second of misses, which is the window only if the rebuild took a whole second.

prompt: Which techniques reduce the number of database queries during a stampede on one key? Select all that apply.

options.text: A short-lived rebuild lock taken with SET NX PX
In-process request coalescing such as Go's singleflight
Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)
Doubling the number of cache nodes in the cluster

explanation: A lock lets one caller rebuild while the others wait and re-read. Coalescing merges concurrent fetches within each process. Early expiration refreshes the key before it expires, so the miss never happens. More cache nodes does nothing: the expired key still lives on one node and every miss still goes to the database.

prompt: Why must a rebuild lock have an expiry (for example PX 5000)?

options.text: So a crashed lock holder cannot block rebuilds of that key forever
Because Redis rejects SET NX without an expiry, so the lock call would fail
So the cached value and the lock expire together and the rebuild starts fresh
To guarantee that only one rebuild of the key ever happens across the cluster

explanation: If the winner crashes after taking the lock, nobody would ever rebuild the key without an expiry. Redis accepts SET NX without an expiry, so that is not the reason. The lock and the cached value have independent TTLs; the lock expiry has nothing to do with when the value expires. And an expiring lock allows another rebuild later, the opposite of 'one rebuild ever'.

prompt: What is the best primary defence?
scenario: Logs show 4,000 requests a second for /users/<id> with random IDs that never repeat and never exist. Every one misses the cache and queries the database.

options.text: Cache a NULL marker for each missing ID with a 60-second TTL so repeats are served
A Bloom filter of valid IDs checked before the cache, plus per-client rate limiting
Increase the TTL of all cached users so the cache covers more of the ID space
Add a local in-process cache on each app server in front of the shared cache

explanation: This is cache penetration with never-repeated IDs. A Bloom filter rejects almost all non-existent IDs without touching the cache or database, and rate limiting makes scanning expensive. NULL markers only help when the same missing ID is asked again; here each marker is used once and just wastes memory. Longer TTLs on real users do nothing for IDs that were never cached. A local cache also only stores things that exist, so random IDs miss it too.

prompt: A Bloom filter says an ID is 'possibly present'. What do you know?

options.text: It definitely exists, because a Bloom filter never reports an ID that was not added
It probably exists but may be a false positive, so check the cache and database
It is missing from the cache but definitely in the database, so skip the cache
The filter is saturated and must be rebuilt before its answers can be trusted

explanation: Bloom filters have false positives but no false negatives, so 'possibly present' must be checked against the real data. 'Definitely exists' ignores false positives: bits set by other IDs can match. The filter knows nothing about what is in the cache, so it cannot tell you to skip it, and it cannot promise the database has the row. A positive answer is normal operation and says nothing about the filter needing a rebuild.

prompt: Which change fixes this most directly?
scenario: A flash-sale product key receives 250,000 reads a second. The cache cluster has 12 nodes and one node is at 100% CPU while the other 11 are below 20%. The product data changes once an hour.

options.text: Add 12 more cache nodes so the key's traffic is spread across 24 nodes
Cache the product in each application server's memory with a 2-second TTL
Increase the key's TTL in the shared cache so it is refreshed less often
Switch the cluster's eviction policy to LRU so the hot key is never evicted

explanation: This is a hot key: one key lives on one node, so a local cache with a short TTL absorbs the reads and the cache node sees roughly one read per app server per TTL. Since data changes hourly, 2 seconds of staleness is fine. More nodes do not split one key; it still hashes to a single node. A longer TTL does not reduce reads, which are already hits. The eviction policy decides what to remove when memory is full, not how reads spread, and the key is not being evicted.

prompt: What is the main cost of replicating a hot key as post:42#0 to post:42#7?

options.text: Every read must query all eight copies and merge them, so read latency rises
Every write must update all eight copies, and copies can briefly disagree
The copies can no longer carry TTLs, so they must be deleted by hand on update
Each read needs a Bloom filter check first to find which copy actually exists

explanation: Key replication spreads reads across nodes but multiplies writes and opens a window where copies differ. Reads are not slower: each read picks one copy at random and hits only that one. Each copy can have its own TTL like any other key. Every copy exists by construction, so no Bloom filter is needed; Bloom filters address penetration and are unrelated.

prompt: What is the most likely cause and fix?
scenario: Every day at 10:00 the database spikes to full CPU for about a minute. A warm-up job loads 2 million keys into the cache at 09:00 each morning with SET ... EX 3600.

options.text: A hot key overloading one node at peak traffic; add a local in-process cache
Synchronised expiry (an avalanche); add random jitter to the TTL
Cache penetration from the warm-up job's keys; add a Bloom filter of valid IDs
The cache is too small for 2 million keys and is evicting; add more memory

explanation: All 2 million keys share one write time and one TTL, so they expire together an hour later and the misses land on the database: an avalanche. Jitter (for example 3,600 ± 10%) spreads expiry over minutes. A hot key is a single key, not a daily spike tied to the warm-up schedule. Penetration involves keys that never exist, but the warm-up keys are real. A cache that is too small would evict throughout the day, not cause a spike precisely one TTL after warming.

prompt: A cache cluster restarts empty while serving 100,000 requests a second. Which measures limit the damage? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warm the cache from a list of hot keys before routing traffic
Rate-limit or circuit-break database reads and cap client retries
Replicate the cache across availability zones
Lower every TTL to 1 second so stale entries from before the restart cannot linger

explanation: Warming restores the hit rate before load arrives; rate limits and circuit breakers stop retries piling onto a struggling database; cross-zone replication means one failure does not empty the cache. Lowering TTLs makes the cache hold less and miss more, which increases database load, and an empty cache has no stale entries to worry about anyway.

prompt: In XFetch, why does a key with a longer rebuild time (larger delta) refresh earlier?

options.text: The early-refresh term scales with delta, so slow rebuilds start further ahead of expiry
XFetch gives keys with longer rebuilds a shorter TTL, so they expire and refresh sooner
delta counts concurrent readers, so busier keys roll the refresh dice more often per second
It doesn't; delta only sets the rebuild lock's timeout, not when a refresh is triggered

explanation: The check is now − delta × beta × ln(random()) ≥ expiry, so a larger delta pushes the effective time later and refreshes start sooner, giving slow rebuilds time to complete before expiry. XFetch does not change the TTL. delta is the measured rebuild time, not a reader count. XFetch uses no lock at all, so delta cannot be a lock timeout.
